About: Projectile Motion — Independent x and y

Source

Simulation
Projectile Motion — Independent x and y (live launch + vertical-twin race + range-vs-angle function plot).
Concept
Horizontal and vertical projectile motions are independent: x(t) = v₀cosθ·t at constant velocity; y(t) = v₀sinθ·t − ½gt² under gravity alone (SI units, g = 9.81 m/s²).
Serves
Component decomposition of 2-D motion; R = v₀²sin2θ/g peaking at 45° (R_max = v₀²/g); complementary angles (30°/60°) give equal range. Kernel-verified anchors: 25 m/s @ 40° → R = 62.74 m, T = 3.28 s, H = 13.16 m; 30° vs 60° → 55.17 m = 55.17 m; 45° → 63.71 m.
Inquiry
Does the tie-line between the projectile and its vertical twin ever tilt as v₀ grows? Which velocity arrow changes in flight? Which angle maximizes range, and why do θ and 90°−θ land at the same spot but at different times?
Misconception
"Horizontal and vertical motions influence each other — a faster horizontal throw falls more slowly." Encoded as prediction choice A, refuted by the observed dead-tie twin race; the falsified coupled equation (a_y = −g·sinθ) appears dashed in the Formal section.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Launch a projectile

Ball A flies at v₀ = 25 m/s, θ = 40°. Watch the amber horizontal velocity arrow stay fixed while the blue vertical arrow drains, flips, and regrows — gravity edits only vy.

2 · Predict — the twin race

Same instant: twin B is tossed straight up with the same vertical speed v₀sinθ, but zero horizontal velocity. Who hits the ground first?

3 · Watch the twin race

Twin B is on. Press 🚀 Launch if needed and watch the dashed tie-line between A and B — it stays level the whole flight. The landing flags show identical times.

4 · Where is the longest shot?

At θ = 45°, range R = v₀²sin2θ/g peaks (sin2θ = 1). At v₀ = 25 m/s that’s R ≈ 63.7 m. Sweep θ and watch the R badge — or open 📈 Range vs angle below.

5 · Same range, different hang time

θ = 30° with ⧉ 90°−θ also launching at 60°. Equal landing spots (sin2θ is symmetric about 45°) — but the steeper ball lands later: more vy buys hang time.

6 · Independence is the law

The myth would need gravity to be diluted by horizontal motion (ay = −g·sinθ) — but every fall you just watched used the full g. Real projectiles fall at g regardless of horizontal speed — that absence of vₓ in y(t) is the independence.

Exact values for the current sliders (✓ model): T = 2v₀sinθ/g, H = (v₀sinθ)²/2g, R = v₀²sin2θ/g, with g = 9.81 m/s².

Horizontal: no horizontal force ⇒ constant velocity. Gravity never touches x.
Vertical: free fall. vₓ does not appear anywhere in y(t) — that absence is the independence.
Hang time and peak height come from the vertical component alone — the twin ball shares both exactly.
Range: constant vₓ times the vertical clock. Peaks at θ = 45° (sin2θ = 1 ⇒ Rmax = v₀²/g).
Complementary angles land at the same spot — 30° and 60° share R (55.17 m at v₀ = 25 m/s) but not T.
⚠ The falsified "coupled" model behind the myth: hang time independent of angle, flat throws never land — refuted by every real fall.

The Physics

Projectile Motion — Independent x and y · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A cannon on level ground fires a ball with launch speed v0 at angle θ above the horizontal. After the shot only gravity acts on the ball. You choose v0 and θ, fire, and read off how long it flies, how high it climbs and where it lands.

What you'll learn

  • How to split a launch velocity into a horizontal part and a vertical part.
  • How flight time, peak height and range follow from v0 and θ.
  • How the range formula compares one launch angle with another.
The apparatus: a cannon at the origin, a launch speed v0 and an angle θ above the ground.

What's on screen

  • Ball A, fired from the cannon, with two small arrows on it in flight, one for each part of its velocity.
  • Launcher preview: the long arrow is v0, the dashed arrows are its two parts, and the angle is labelled.
  • Landing flag where a ball touches down, with its flight time and range.
  • Readouts panel: time since launch, and the range of the last landing.
See itFire the cannon at v0 = 25 m/s and θ = 40°. Watch for: one arc from the cannon to a landing flag that carries the flight time and the range.

03

Horizontal and vertical motion run separately

Gravity pulls straight down, so it changes only the vertical velocity. Nothing pushes sideways, so the horizontal velocity stays what it was at launch. Split the launch velocity into its two parts:

vx = v0cosθ    vy0 = v0sinθ
vx never changes. vy = vy0 − gt changes by 9.81 m/s every second.

Each part then has its own equation of motion:

x(t) = v0cosθ · t    y(t) = v0sinθ · t − ½gt²
The symbol vx appears in x(t) only. It is absent from y(t).

At v0 = 25 m/s and θ = 40°, vx = 19.15 m/s and vy0 = 16.07 m/s. After 1 s the vertical velocity has fallen to +6.26 m/s, after 2 s it is −3.55 m/s, and after 3 s it is −13.36 m/s. Positive means rising, negative means falling.

See itFire the cannon at 25 m/s and 40°. Watch for: the amber horizontal arrow on the ball keeping its length while the blue vertical arrow shrinks, flips to point down and grows again.
04

Hang time and peak height come from the vertical motion alone

The ball lands when y(t) returns to zero, which gives t(vy0 − ½gt) = 0. At the top vy = 0, which happens at half that time. So

T = 2v0sinθ / g    H = (v0sinθ)² / 2g
Neither formula contains vx or cosθ.

At 25 m/s and 40°, T = 3.276 s and H = 13.162 m. Ball B, the twin, is tossed straight up with the same vy0 = 16.07 m/s and no sideways speed. Its y(t) is identical to A's, so it has the same T and the same H. Ball A covers 62.7 m along the ground in that time, and B none, yet both land together.

Sideways speed does not shorten or lengthen the fall.

See itTurn on Twin ball and fire at 25 m/s and 40°. Watch for: the dashed tie-line between B and A staying level all flight, and both landing flags reading 3.28 s.
05

Range is horizontal speed times hang time and peaks at 45°

The ball moves sideways at constant vx for the whole time T, so R = vxT. Using 2 sinθ cosθ = sin 2θ,

R = v0cosθ · T = v0² sin 2θ / g
R grows as the square of v0: doubling the speed quadruples the range.

sin 2θ can never exceed 1, and it equals 1 at θ = 45°. So the range at a given speed is largest there, Rmax = v0² / g. At 25 m/s that is 63.71 m, while 40° gives 62.74 m. At 50 m/s and 45° the range is 254.84 m, four times as much.

v0 θ

These sliders move the sim's sliders too. Press Launch to fire.

See itSet the angle to 45° and fire at 25 m/s. Watch for: the landing flag reading 63.71 m, the longest range at this speed.
06

Complementary angles land together but hang for different times

Replace θ by 90° − θ. Then sin(2(90° − θ)) = sin(180° − 2θ) = sin 2θ, so the range does not change:

R(θ) = R(90° − θ)
At a fixed speed, two angles that add up to 90° share one landing point.

At 25 m/s, 30° and 60° both land 55.17 m away. Their hang times differ, because T = 2v0sinθ / g and sin 60° is larger than sin 30°: 4.41 s against 2.55 s. The steeper ball starts with vy0 = 21.65 m/s instead of 12.50 m/s, so it rises higher (23.89 m against 7.96 m) and stays up longer.

At θ = 45° the two angles coincide, which is why the peak sits in the middle.

See itSet the angle to 30°, turn on 90°−θ and fire at 25 m/s. Watch for: two arcs ending at the same flag, labelled equal range 55.17 m, with the steeper ball M landing later.
07

Where it matters

  • A ball rolling off a table. Whatever its sideways speed, it reaches the floor after the same time as a ball dropped from the table edge.
  • A fire hose. At a fixed nozzle speed, a flat jet and a high lobbed jet whose angles add to 90° hit the same spot on the ground. The flat jet arrives sooner.
  • Sport. A shot-putter releases the shot above ground level, so the best angle falls a little below 45°. This sim launches from the ground, where the best angle is exactly 45°.
  • Real air. Air resistance acts against the whole velocity. With it, the horizontal and vertical motions no longer separate as cleanly, and the ideal formulas become approximations.
08

Summary

In one line. A projectile is a body launched at an angle and then moved by gravity alone, and its hang time, peak height and range all follow from v0 and θ.

Key points

  • x(t) = v0cosθ · t at constant vx, and y(t) = v0sinθ · t − ½gt². The symbol vx is absent from y(t).
  • T = 2v0sinθ / g, H = (v0sinθ)² / 2g and R = v0² sin 2θ / g.
  • R peaks at 45°, where R = v0² / g, and R(θ) = R(90° − θ).

Common mix-ups

  • "A faster sideways throw falls more slowly." The fall depends on vy0 only. The twin tossed straight up lands at the same time.
  • "A steeper angle always goes farther." At 25 m/s, 80° lands at 21.79 m and 40° at 62.74 m.
  • "Equal ranges mean equal flight times." 30° and 60° both reach 55.17 m, after 2.55 s and 4.41 s.

Things to try on your own

  • Set 50 m/s and 45°, predict R, then fire and compare with the flag.
  • Pick two angles that add to 90°, such as 25° and 65°, and test that they land together.
  • Turn on Twin ball at θ = 70° and compare the two landing times.
